## License

jim-ph's Freesound pack "vintage keyboard" (https://freesound.org/people/jim-ph/packs/12363/) has five sounds. On 2026-10-02 each sound's Freesound page showed **CC0 1.0** (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/), which allows copying, modifying and distributing, including commercially, without permission or credit; the pack page lists all five as "Creative Commons 0" too. The pack is `CC0-1.0`; the credit in `pack.json` is a courtesy. The description (a keystroke of a 1986 DOS mechanical keyboard, recorded with a condenser microphone) is from the Freesound pages.

## Where the files came from

Freesound needs a login to download, so the files come from the MIT-licensed Tickeys app, which ships the pack unchanged with Freesound's own `license.txt` (https://github.com/yingDev/Tickeys/tree/028083403ab75eae752446ce30cffb3b22b49eab/Tickeys.app/Contents/Resources/data/mechanical). That license.txt lists the five sounds, each as Creative Commons 0. Tickeys renamed them `1.wav` … `5.wav`; each is matched to its Freesound sound by the duration and file size the Freesound page lists. Only this folder of Tickeys is used: its other sound folders have no stated origin.

## Each take is a whole keystroke

Every recording holds one keystroke: the key-down, then the key-up 120–170 ms later, with a quiet gap between them. Played whole on key-down, each would also sound a key-up at a fixed delay, whenever the key is actually released. So the build splits each take in two (`packlib.split_tap`): the key-up is the loudest moment at least 60 ms after the key-down starts, its attack starts where the level (1 ms frames, walking back from that peak) first drops 20 dB below it, and the split is the middle of the quietest 5 ms between 30 ms after the key-down and 1 ms before that attack. The build stops unless that gap is at least 24 dB (RMS) below the key-up's peak. The key-down becomes the press sound and the same take's key-up its release sound: every release is a recorded key-up, none is made up. The key-up sound starts 5 ms before its attack (or at the split, if that is later); what lies between the split and there (up to 37 ms, a soft noise in some takes) is left out, so that no key-up starts that far ahead of its click. Both strokes are cut against the whole take's noise floor.

## How each file was made

All files: decoded at 44100 Hz (the recordings' own rate, mono), 30 Hz 2nd-order Butterworth high-pass (also removes DC), split into key-down and key-up as above, each stroke cut as listed (0.5 ms raised-cosine fade-in before the onset; raised-cosine fade-out ending on an exact zero; at most 0.4 s), one gain of -4.71 dB for the whole pack (the key-downs' median peak goes to -6 dBFS; the strokes keep their natural differences, and each key-up its level next to its own key-down), written as 16-bit PCM WAV. No other processing. Headroom: the loudest file's true peak (4x oversampled) is -5.45 dBFS, and -4.78 dBFS at the top of the runtime's ±8% volume variation (the rule is at most -1 dBFS, as the mixer clips hard at 0 dBFS), so no headroom trim was needed.

The strongest key-down (Vintage Keyboard 4) is only 2.8 dB above the median of the others (or brighter than them), below the 3 dB rule, so there is no separate space bar sound and every key uses the same variants.

`preview.wav` (SHA-256 `137b42610b75496f8389f54c1e7157b0e4817abe5de7256d41056f7d57c1f8ad`): just under 2 s of typing rendered from the pack's own files (4 keys, space, 3 keys, space, 3 keys, Enter, each with its key-up; 60–120 ms holds, 80–200 ms between presses, ±8% volume per stroke, fixed random seed; Space and Enter use the same strokes as every other key, as in the pack), scaled down only if it would peak above -1 dBFS.

## Loudness

`volume` in `pack.json` is 0.88 (-1.1 dB): a playback gain the app applies to the whole pack, so no audio file changes. Typing loudness is matched across the bundled packs so that switching packs does not jump in volume; the target is TakTak's reference typing level, -25.8 LK. Measured with `cargo run -p synth-packs --release -- loudness packs/vintage-keyboard` (`tools/synth-packs/src/loudness.rs`): the K-weighted (ITU-R BS.1770) energy of the first 100 ms of the sample each alphanumeric key plays on press by default, power-averaged over the keys, on the samples as the app loads them at 48 kHz. The pack reads -24.7 LK as built and -25.8 LK at this volume; the loudest true peak at the top of the volume variation becomes -5.90 dBFS. `build.py` writes the volume (`VOLUME`), so a rebuild keeps it.
